response.question: Someone is selling products with my registered trademark on them. What can I do?
response.answer:
This may be trade mark infringement, but selling products with your mark is not automatically infringement. It depends on the goods, how the mark is used, and whether the use is permitted. Offering goods for sale under a registered mark counts as use of the mark. [trade_marks_act_1999:29]

For example, resale of lawfully acquired goods put on the market by you or with your consent is not infringement for that reason alone. The position may differ if you have legitimate reasons to oppose further sales, such as the goods being changed or impaired. [trade_marks_act_1999:30]

If there is infringement, a valid registration gives its owner a right to obtain relief, subject to the applicable conditions and limitations. The sources provided do not explain the specific remedies or procedure for an ordinary infringement claim. [trade_marks_act_1999:28]

response.question: Can I sue someone for using my brand name if I never registered it?
response.answer:
Yes, you may be able to sue even if you never registered your brand name. A possible claim is called “passing off”. The law recognises protection for an unregistered trade mark used in business and refers to passing-off suits involving an identical or deceptively similar mark [trade_marks_act_1999:11] [trade_marks_act_1999:134].

A court may grant an order to stop the use, and may also award compensation or an account of profits, subject to legal limitations [trade_marks_act_1999:135]. This is general legal information, not legal advice.

response.question: Why could my trademark application be rejected?
response.answer:
A trademark application could be refused for several reasons. The reasons most relevant to you depend on your mark and the goods or services in your application.

• The mark does not distinguish your goods or services from others, or it consists only of descriptive or commonly used terms. However, it may avoid refusal on these grounds if it became distinctive through use before you applied, or is well known. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• The mark could deceive or confuse the public, hurt religious sensitivities, or contains scandalous or obscene material. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• The mark consists only of certain shapes, such as a shape necessary to achieve a technical result. [trade_marks_act_1999:9]
• It conflicts with an earlier identical or similar trademark for identical or similar goods or services, and there is a likelihood of public confusion. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• It is identical or similar to an earlier trademark that is well known in India. This can matter even for different goods or services, if use of your mark without good reason would unfairly benefit from or harm the earlier mark’s distinctiveness or reputation. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]
• Use of the mark could be prevented by an earlier right, such as protection for an unregistered trademark used in trade or copyright. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

For the well-known mark and earlier-right grounds in the last two points, an objection must be raised by the earlier trademark’s owner in opposition proceedings—proceedings in which registration is challenged. Consent from the owner of an earlier mark or right may also be relevant. [trade_marks_act_1999:11]

If the Registrar refuses your application, the Registrar must record the reasons and the material used to reach the decision in writing. [trade_marks_act_1999:18]

response.question: How long is a trademark registration valid and how do I renew it?
response.answer:
A trade mark registered after the Act came into force lasts for 10 years. It can be renewed repeatedly, for 10 years at a time, starting from the expiry of the previous registration. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

To renew, the registered owner must apply to the Registrar in the required manner and within the required period, and pay the required fee. The Registrar must send a notice before expiry explaining the expiry date and renewal conditions. The supplied sources do not specify the ordinary application deadline, form or fee amount. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

If the registration has expired, an application in the required form, with the fee and an extra charge, can be made within six months of expiry. The Registrar must then renew it and must not remove it from the register. If the mark was removed for non-payment, the owner may apply for restoration after six months and within one year of expiry. Restoration is subject to the Registrar being satisfied that it is fair to restore it. [trade_marks_act_1999:25]

Special expiry provisions apply to marks registered before the Act came into force, so check the registration record if yours is an older mark. [trade_marks_act_1999:159]

response.question: Can I use a song in my YouTube video without permission?

Whether your use qualifies depends on the circumstances; simply calling a video a review does not settle the question. For criticism or review, the law also requires an acknowledgment identifying the work and, subject to exceptions, its author. [copyright_act_1957:52]

response.question: How long does copyright last for a book after the author dies?
response.answer:
For a book published during the author’s lifetime, copyright generally lasts for 60 years from 1 January of the year after the author dies. For example, if the author died in 2000, the term runs until the end of 2060. [copyright_act_1957:22]

For a jointly authored book, the period is normally calculated from the death of the last surviving author. [copyright_act_1957:22]

Different rules can apply if the book is published anonymously or under a pen name. [copyright_act_1957:23] If it is first published after the author’s death, the calculation can also be different; an earlier published adaptation may matter. [copyright_act_1957:24]

response.question: My employer says they own the articles I wrote at work. Who owns the copyright?
response.answer:
It depends on your job, why you wrote the articles and any agreement you made.

Generally, if you wrote them in the course of your employment, your employer is the first copyright owner unless you agreed otherwise. Being the first owner means owning the copyright when it initially arises. [copyright_act_1957:17]

There is a special rule for articles written while employed by the proprietor of a newspaper, magazine or similar periodical, for publication in one. Unless you agreed otherwise, the proprietor is the first owner of the rights to publish the article in such a periodical or reproduce it for that purpose. You are the first owner in other respects. [copyright_act_1957:17]

Without knowing your employer’s business, your role and your agreement, it is not possible to say which rule applies to you.

response.question: What is the jail punishment for copyright piracy?
response.answer:
For knowingly infringing copyright, or helping someone do so, the usual punishment is jail for six months to three years, plus a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business, the court may impose less than six months’ jail or a fine below ₹50,000, giving special reasons in its judgment.

For a second or later conviction for the same offence, the usual punishment is one to three years’ jail and a fine of ₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh. A similar exception applies where the infringement was not for gain in the course of trade or business.

A different rule applies to knowingly using a pirated computer program: the usual punishment is seven days to three years’ jail and a fine of ₹50,000 to ₹2 lakh. If it was not used for gain or in the course of trade or business, the court may, for special reasons, impose no jail sentence and a fine of up to ₹50,000.

response.question: Can someone challenge or oppose my patent?

• Before grant: Once your application is published, any person can oppose the grant in writing to the Controller, the patent authority. [patents_act_1970:25]

Examples of grounds for opposition include that the invention was publicly known or used in India before the relevant priority date, was obvious, or was not clearly and sufficiently described. The priority date is the relevant date used to assess a patent claim. [patents_act_1970:25]

For a post-grant opposition, the Controller must give you and the opponent an opportunity to be heard. The Controller may then maintain, amend or revoke the patent. [patents_act_1970:25]

response.question: What exclusive rights does copyright give me over my novel?
response.answer:
If you own the copyright in your novel, you generally have the exclusive right to do the following yourself or allow others to do them. These rights cover the whole novel or a substantial part of it, and are subject to legal limits. [copyright_act_1957:14]

• Make copies, including digital copies. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Issue copies to the public, except copies already in circulation. A copy sold once is considered already in circulation. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Perform the novel in public or make it available to the public. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Make a film or sound recording of it. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Translate it. [copyright_act_1957:14]
• Adapt it, for example by making a shortened version or turning it into a play. [copyright_act_1957:14; copyright_act_1957:2]
• Exercise these rights over a translation or adaptation too. [copyright_act_1957:14]

These rights are not absolute. For example, fair dealing for personal use, research, criticism or review can be permitted. Whether a use is fair depends on the circumstances. [copyright_act_1957:52]

Separately, as the author, you have the right to claim authorship and to seek a remedy for changes to the work that harm your honour or reputation, even if you transfer your copyright. [copyright_act_1957:57]

A seller may avoid punishment if they prove one of the specified defences. response.question: How long does copyright protection last in India?

- Books, plays, music and artistic works published during the author’s lifetime: generally 60 years from the beginning of the year after the author dies. For a work with joint authors, the period is counted from the year after the last author dies. [copyright_act_1957:22]
- Films: 60 years from the beginning of the year after publication. [copyright_act_1957:26]
- Works published without the author’s name or under a pen name: the period is generally 60 years from the beginning of the year after first publication. If the author’s identity is disclosed before that period expires, it is instead counted from the beginning of the year after the author dies. [copyright_act_1957:23]
- Government works and public-undertaking works: where the government or public undertaking was the first copyright owner, the period is 60 years from the beginning of the year after first publication. [copyright_act_1957:28] [copyright_act_1957:28A]

Similarity alone does not necessarily mean the other person has infringed your rights. The details matter.

response.question: Can my product's packaging or colour scheme be protected as a trademark?

Registration can be limited to a combination of colours. If a trade mark is registered without a colour limitation, it is treated as registered for all colours. This does not mean you automatically own every use of those colours.

A similar earlier trade mark may also prevent registration if the similarity and the goods involved are likely to confuse the public.
